A.explanation: Point A is just before impact where speed is maximum downward, so the ball is at the ground, not at maximum height.

B.explanation: Point B is just after the bounce where velocity reverses sign, so the ball is still at the ground moving upward fastest.

C.explanation: Point C is where velocity is $0$ during the upward flight, so the ball momentarily stops at the top of the bounce.

D.explanation: Point D is just before the second impact where downward speed is maximum again, so the ball is back at the ground.

hints: Notice where the graph jumps from positive velocity at A to negative velocity at B - this sudden sign change marks the bounce off the surface.
Follow the straight line from B upward: the velocity becomes less negative as gravity slows the upward motion, so think about what the velocity value must be at the very top.
Maximum height after the first bounce means the ball momentarily stops before falling again, so look for $v = 0$ on the time axis between the two bounces.
walkthrough: The first sloping line from $0$ to A shows velocity increasing steadily while falling, with constant gradient equal to acceleration due to gravity.
At A the velocity suddenly changes sign to B. This vertical jump is the bounce, where direction reverses from downward to upward while the ball is in contact with the surface.
From B the graph is a straight line of the same gradient, showing the ball slowing as it rises because gravity acts downward opposite to the upward motion.
Maximum height is reached when the upward motion stops for an instant before the ball starts to fall, which is the condition $v = 0$.
On the graph the line from B crosses the time axis at C, where velocity is zero between the first and second bounces. This is option C
